The densest lecture of the course. We fold two stories into one: (A) the brain's ventral visual stream, and (B) the convolutional network as its engineered embodiment. Quantitative model–brain comparison (RSA) is L12; XAI is L13. We only forward-point to those today.

L10 ended on the punchline that a sparse/efficient code of natural images yields Gabor-like V1 receptive fields — the objective predicts the biology. Today we take that as given and build upward, then show the CNN is the architecture that does the same thing.

This is the target the rest of the lecture explains. Rapid categorization pushes the visual system to its temporal limit, so recognition has to ride on the most elementary, feedforward building blocks of vision before eye movements / attention / memory kick in.

Optional / fast slide — cut if running short. The point is just that the center-surround computation is doing real work and we can see its signature in perception.

Optional / fast slide.

CALLBACK, NOT INTRODUCTION (added 2026-08-06). "Tangled manifolds made linearly separable" is stated three separate times across the course — in L05 as the computational problem of vision, in L08 as what a hidden layer does for XOR, and here as what the ventral stream does. Students previously met all three with no indication they were the same idea. Name it: "this is the third time we have said this sentence, and that is the point." L05 said a good representation untangles; L08 showed a hidden layer doing it on a toy problem; this slide says the brain does it over four cortical areas and about 100 milliseconds. L09's generalization figure is the same picture with labeled examples added, so the phrasing there should match the phrasing here.

Per-element: F[l]_{i,j,c} = f( sum_{u,v,c'} K_{u,v,c',c} F[l-1]_{i+u,j+v,c'} + b_c ) — a local dot product (template match) reused at every (i,j). Notation matches the cheat-sheet conv-layer line.

The deck has done brain→AI richly (efficient coding → Gabors → HMAX → CNN). This is the clean AI→brain example: a task-optimized model used as a causal hypothesis generator, designing stimuli that control neural activity. Quantitative model–brain comparison itself is L12; this is the causal/synthesis flavor that L12 does not cover.

Added 2026-08-03. The methodological point is the important one: in both the CSF and the crowding studies the authors ran a 2AFC paradigm on the network — same task, same stimuli, same staircase logic as human psychophysics — rather than inventing a new model-only metric. That is the "psychophysics of the model" idea that returns in L13 and L19. The pattern in the scorecard is worth a minute of discussion: the signatures that come for free are the ones a filtering-and-pooling front end would produce anyway. The one that does NOT come for free (shape bias) is the one that requires integrating information globally. Ask the class to predict which side a new phenomenon would fall on before you tell them. Don't overclaim the CSF result: the networks' CSFs are characteristically human-LIKE in shape, not identical, and depend on the training task.
